article.title: Survivorship Bias: Learning Only from the Winners
article.why: Practical analytical English for data-driven decisions.

paragraphs.en: Survivorship bias appears when an analysis focuses on cases that remain visible after a selection process and ignores cases that disappeared. The classic logic is simple: if we study only successful companies, active customers, completed projects, or products still on the market, we may mistake characteristics of survivors for causes of success. Imagine analyzing customers who have held a credit card for five years. They may show high engagement and frequent spending. But customers who canceled earlier are absent from the dataset. If we conclude that the observed behavior describes all customers over five years, we have conditioned on survival. The same problem appears in investment analysis when failed funds disappear from historical comparisons, in employee studies when only current workers answer a survey, and in product analytics when churned users are excluded from engagement metrics. Survivorship bias is not solved by collecting more records from survivors. A million surviving cases can still represent the wrong population. Analysts should define the population at the beginning of the process and track what happens to every eligible unit, including exits. Cohort analysis is useful because it starts with a fixed group and follows both retained and lost members over time. Administrative data may also preserve information about canceled accounts or failed applications. When missing cases cannot be recovered, the limitation should be stated explicitly. Weighting or statistical adjustment may help in some settings, but only when the selection mechanism is sufficiently understood and relevant information is available. Communication should match the evidence. “Among customers who remained active for five years, spending was high” is descriptive and defensible. “Long-term customers naturally become high spenders” implies a broader mechanism that the survivor-only data cannot establish. The practical question is always: who had a chance to appear in this dataset, and who disappeared before measurement? Analysts should define the population, observation window, decision rule, and operational constraint before interpreting the metric. paragraphs.zh: 繁中完整翻譯與解說：本文強調分析結果必須放回正確的 baseline、母體、segment、decision cost 與資料生成機制中理解。百分比、總體 KPI、model threshold 或部署後的新資料，都可能因分母、selection、population mix 或舊 policy 而改變含義。
paragraphs.ja: 日本語完全訳・解説：分析結果はbaseline、母集団、segment、decision cost、data generating mechanismと結び付けて解釈する必要がある。percentage、集計KPI、model threshold、deployment後のdataは、分母、selection、population mix、過去policyによって意味が変わり得る。
